title: Resonant multi-harmonic acousto-optics for programmable frequency control of visible light in a CMOS platform
authors: Jacob M. Freedman, Matthew J. Storey, Daniel Dominguez, Andrew Leenheer, Nils T. Otterstrom, Matt Eichenfield
abstract: Scaling quantum control for atoms, ions, and solid-state emitters requires gigahertz-frequency spectral control of high-power visible light in a volume-manufacturable platform. Silicon nitride photonics provides high power handling and CMOS-foundry compatibility but has no intrinsic mechanism for high-speed modulation. Integration with piezoelectric materials enables acousto-optic phase modulation, and mechanical resonant enhancement has made it efficient at gigahertz frequencies. However, a single resonance restricts the modulation waveform to a single tone, imposing Bessel-function sideband amplitudes and limiting frequency-shifting efficiency to 33.9%. Here we engineer a silicon nitride acousto-optic microstructure to support harmonically spaced resonances at 1.14 GHz and 2.28 GHz, each strongly optomechanically coupled to a 730 nm guided optical mode, so that tailored non-sinusoidal modulation waveforms can be resonantly synthesized. By piezoelectrically controlling the two mechanical amplitudes and their relative phase, we demonstrate 50% conversion to one sideband (1.5x the single-tone theoretical maximum), a flat seven-line comb, and a frequency shift with 60 dB carrier and 53 dB image suppression - to our knowledge the highest reported for an integrated modulator. The devices are fabricated in a 200 mm CMOS foundry, and we measure 91.7% yield without post-fabrication tuning across 36 devices from three wafers. We also show how the technique can be straightforwardly scaled to three or more harmonics. This result overcomes the trade-off between resonant enhancement and spectral programmability, with important consequences including improved single-qubit gate efficiency for hyperfine qubits.
summary: This paper presents a novel acousto-optic modulator design on a CMOS platform that overcomes the spectral limitations of single-frequency modulation. By engineering the structure to support multiple, harmonically spaced resonances, the authors can synthesize complex, non-sinusoidal light waveforms. This breakthrough significantly enhances frequency control for visible light, making it highly relevant for scaling quantum gate operations.
main_problem: Scaling quantum control for atomic, ionic, and solid-state emitters requires high-power, gigahertz-frequency spectral control of visible light in a manufacturable platform.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a method using harmonically spaced resonances to achieve programmable, non-sinusoidal modulation waveforms, significantly improving frequency-shifting efficiency and suppression levels compared to single-tone systems.
method: They engineered a silicon nitride microstructure to support multiple, harmonically spaced mechanical resonances, which are then piezoelectrically controlled to synthesize complex modulation signals.
model_or_system: The physical system is an acousto-optic modulator fabricated on a 200 mm CMOS platform using silicon nitride photonics integrated with an aluminum nitride piezoelectric actuator. The modulation relies on coupling multiple mechanical resonances to a guided visible-wavelength optical mode.
key_observables: Conversion efficiency (up to 50% sideband conversion), frequency shift suppression (60 dB carrier, 53 dB image suppression), and the ability to generate flat multi-line frequency combs.
important_parameters: Harmonically spaced resonance frequencies (e.g., 1.14 GHz and 2.28 GHz), modulation depths ($ eta_n$), and relative phase control.
main_assumptions: The technique overcomes the spectral limitation imposed by single-tone modulation by utilizing multiple, harmonically spaced resonances, which is shown to be scalable to more harmonics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure, the principle of two-tone harmonic phase modulation, and the resulting spectral comb lines. Supplementary figures detail the theoretical modeling of sideband generation and efficiency optimization.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the need for high-speed, programmable light control for quantum systems. It then proposes the use of multi-harmonic acousto-optics on a CMOS platform. The core work involves demonstrating the synthesis of tailored waveforms and achieving record suppression levels, concluding with discussions on scalability and quantum applications.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical hardware bottleneck in quantum computing: generating high-fidelity, high-frequency optical control signals. The demonstrated high efficiency and manufacturability are crucial for integrating quantum light sources with classical photonic infrastructure.
